title: New level of evidence grading system for Guidelines, artificial intelligence, and adult congenital heart disease
abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. Guidelines play an important role in fulfilling the mission of scientific societies. In the past 2 years, nine Guidelines have been published by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC).1–8 This Focus Issue opens with two Special Articles which revise the level of evidence (LOE) grading system for Guideline recommendations. The first Special Article is entitled ‘2024 Revision of the level of evidence grading system for ESC clinical practice guideline recommendations I: therapy and prevention’ by Peter Jüni from the University of Oxford, UK, and colleagues.9 The LOE grading system for ESC Clinical Practice Guidelines classifies the quality of the evidence supporting a recommendation. However, the current taxonomy does not fully consider the optimal study design necessary to establish evidence for such recommendations. Therefore, two separate taskforces of clinical and methodological experts were appointed by the Clinical Practice Guidelines Committee, with the first tasked with updating the LOE grading system for therapy and prevention, and the second responsible for developing an LOE grading system for diagnosis and prediction. The updated system for therapy and prevention presented here maintains the three-level grading structure but uses revised definitions. Level of evidence A represents conclusive evidence usually from ≥2 adequately powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) free from major bias, with substantial evidence against the play of chance when combined in a meta-analysis (e.g. P < .005 for superiority). Additional criteria are specified to define substantial evidence against the play of chance in the case of non-inferiority, equivalence, and harm. Level of evidence B is now subdivided into B1 and B2. Level of evidence B1 represents suggestive evidence usually from ≥1 adequately powered RCT free from major bias, or a meta-analysis of such RCTs, with some evidence against the play of chance (e.g. P < .05 for superiority). Level of evidence B2 represents limited evidence from ≥2 adequately powered non-randomized studies with careful control of major sources of bias or from a meta-analysis of small, underpowered RCTs. Level of evidence C represents preliminary evidence from either non-randomized studies without careful control of major sources of bias, a single small, underpowered RCT, or expert consensus (Figure 1). The original and revised level of evidence grading systems. RCT, randomized controlled trial.9 The second Special Article entitled ‘2024 Revision of the level of evidence grading system for ESC clinical practice guideline recommendations II: diagnostic tests and prediction models’ is by Emanuele Di Angelantonio from the University of Cambridge, UK, and colleagues.10 This report develops a new system for diagnostic tests and prediction models which maintains the three-level grading structure to classify the quality of the evidence but introduces new definitions specific for diagnosis and prediction. For diagnostic tests, LOE A represents conclusive evidence of adequate diagnostic ability from at least two high-quality studies. Level of evidence B represents suggestive evidence from one high-quality or at least two moderate-quality studies. Level of evidence C represents preliminary evidence not classified as A or B, including evidence from fewer than two moderate-quality studies, or from expert consensus. For prediction models, LOE A represents conclusive evidence of adequate predictive ability from at least one high-quality derivation and two or more external validation studies of at least moderate quality. Level of evidence B represents suggestive evidence in one or more derivation study and one or more external validation studies of at least moderate quality. Level of evidence C represents preliminary evidence not classified as A or B, including evidence from a derivation study of at least moderate quality, but with low quality or no external validation, or a derivation study of low quality. The Issue continues with a focus on digital health and innovation and congenital heart disease. With the advent of artificial intelligence (AI), novel opportunities arise to revolutionize healthcare delivery and improve population health.11–16 In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Artificial intelligence to improve cardiovascular population health’, Benjamin Meder from the University of Heidelberg, Germany, and colleagues provides a state-of-the-art overview of recent advancements in AI technologies and their applications in enhancing cardiovascular health at the population level.17 From predictive analytics to personalized interventions, AI-driven approaches are increasingly being utilized to analyse vast amounts of healthcare data, uncover disease patterns, and optimize resource allocation. Furthermore, AI-enabled technologies such as wearable devices and remote monitoring systems facilitate continuous cardiac monitoring and early detection of diseases, and promise more timely interventions. Additionally, AI-powered systems aid healthcare professionals in clinical decision-making processes, thereby improving accuracy and treatment effectiveness. By using AI systems to augment existing data sources, such as registries and biobanks, completely new research questions can be addressed to identify novel mechanisms and pharmaceutical targets. Despite this remarkable potential of AI in enhancing population health, challenges related to legal issues, data privacy, algorithm bias, and ethical considerations must be addressed to ensure equitable access and improved outcomes for all individuals. Emerging evidence supports AI-enhanced electrocardiograms (AI-ECGs) for detecting acute myocardial infarction (AMI), but real-world validation is needed.18 In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Artificial intelligence applied to electrocardiogram to rule out acute myocardial infarction: the ROMIAE multicentre study’, Min Sung Lee from Sejong Hospital, Republic of Korea, and colleagues performed a study to evaluate the performance of AI-ECG in detecting AMI in the emergency department (ED). The Rule-Out acute Myocardial Infarction using Artificial intelligence Electrocardiogram analysis (ROMIAE) study is a prospective cohort study conducted in the Republic of Korea from March 2022 to October 2023, involving 18 university-level teaching hospitals. Adult patients presenting to the ED within 24 h of symptom onset with suspected AMI were assessed. Exposure included AI-ECG score, HEART score, GRACE 2.0 score, high-sensitivity troponin level, and Physician AMI score. The primary outcome was diagnosis of AMI during index admission, and the secondary outcome was 30 day major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). The study population comprised 8493 adults, of whom 19% were diagnosed with AMI. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for AI-ECG was 0.878, comparable with the HEART score (0.877) and superior to the GRACE 2.0 score, high-sensitivity troponin level, and Physician AMI score. For predicting 30 day MACE, AI-ECG (AUC 0.866) performed comparably with the HEART score (0.858). The integration of the AI-ECG improved risk stratification and AMI discrimination, with a net reclassification improvement of 20% and a C-index of 0.926, compared with the HEART score alone. The authors conclude that in this multicentre prospective study, AI-ECG demonstrates diagnostic accuracy and predictive power for AMI and 30 day MACE, similar to or better than that of traditional risk stratification methods. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by I-Min Chiu and David Ouyang from Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA, USA.19 The authors point out that the ROMIAE study highlights AI-ECG as a promising innovation for managing AMI, but its full potential in clinical practice requires further evaluation and investigation. Randomized controlled trials are essential to evaluate the real-world impact of these advancements on patient outcomes and healthcare efficiency. Further refinement of AI-ECG algorithms is critical to addressing diagnostic challenges. Integrating AI-ECG with existing clinical scoring systems, such as the HEART score, could enhance its acceptance among clinicians by improving interpretability and trust. This approach leverages the strengths of AI while aligning it with established decision-making frameworks, ensuring a smoother integration into clinical workflows. Indeed, AI-ECG has the potential to transform cardiovascular diagnostics and care by improving workflows and enabling timely, effective interventions. However, successful implementation requires addressing key challenges, such as infrastructure demands, clinician training, and equitable access. By focusing on these areas and generating robust evidence to support its utility, AI-ECG can evolve into a transformative tool that not only enhances diagnostic precision but also advances precision medicine and equitable healthcare delivery. Adults with congenital heart disease who underwent a Fontan palliation are at increased risk of premature death. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘The Fontan Adult Brompton clinical score and mortality risk’, Claudia Montanaro from Imperial College London, UK, and colleagues aimed to identify a risk score based on widely available clinical variables at the first adult visit and facilitate personalized care.20 A single tertiary centre retrospective study included patients with a Fontan circulation during their first outpatient visit as an adult with congenital heart disease. Anatomic and peri-procedural data, clinical, laboratory, and echocardiographic parameters at the first visit, and mortality or heart transplantation data were examined. A stepwise backward conditional approach was used to build a multivariate prognostic model, validated in an external retrospective cohort. Overall, 230 patients (50% female), with a median age of 21.7 years, were included. Within 10.2 years of follow-up, 44 patients died and two received heart transplantation. A score including age at the first visit, history of atrial tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, New York Heart Association class, systolic blood pressure, and resting arterial oxygen saturation was derived, discriminating patients into low, intermediate, and high risk of death or transplantation (C-index: 0.71). Discriminative ability was excellent (C-index 0.92) when externally validated in a cohort of 80 patients (41% female, median age 18.4 years) (Figure 2). The Fontan Adult Brompton (FAB) score. NYHA, New York Heart Association; PLE, protein-losing enteropathy; SBP, systolic blood pressure; SpO2%, arterial oxygen saturation.20 The authors conclude that this novel, readily available, externally validated, clinical score identifies adult patients with a Fontan palliation at risk of mortality or transplantation and can be applied towards personalized care in this growing population with complex congenital heart disease. In a Rapid Communication article entitled ‘Common and divergent cellular aetiologies underlying hypoplastic left heart syndrome and hypoplastic right heart syndrome’, Yang Yu from the Nationwide Children’s Hospital, Columbus, OH, USA, and colleagues, note that single ventricle heart defects (SVHDs) are the most severe forms of congenital heart defects (CHDs) and are classified based on the affected ventricles: hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) and hypoplastic right heart syndrome (HRHS).21 Cellular aetiologies underlying differential left and right ventricular hypoplasia are unknown and remain intractable without an experimental model to probe common and divergent cellular aetiologies between HLHS and HRHS. In this study, the authors leveraged patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and single-cell transcriptomics to interrogate distinct aetiologies of HLHS and HRHS. Both HLHS and HRHS iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) exhibited a reduced proliferation capacity compared with sex-matched family controls under static and cyclic stretch conditions. Biological pathways related to cell cycle progression, DNA replication, and cell proliferation were down-regulated in both HLHS and HRHS iPSC-CMs, suggesting an intrinsic cardiac proliferation deficiency. Single-cell transcriptomics indicated that differentiation of cardiac mesoderm towards second heart field (SHF) progenitors was compromised in both HLHS and HRHS. However, differentiation of epicardial progenitors was enhanced at the expense of first heart field (FHF)/SHF progenitors in HLHS, whereas FHF progenitors were prevalent in HRHS. Trajectory inference analysis uncovers distinct cell lineage determination routes in FHF and SHF progenitors between HLHS and HRHS. Moreover, HLHS iPSC-CMs exhibit reduced mitochondrial activities, whereas HRHS iPSC-CMs show enhanced mitochondrial respiration and ATP production compared with controls. The authors conclude that these common and divergent cellular aetiologies of HLHS and HRHS may underlie ventricular hypoplasia in the left and right side of the heart. title: Survey on Privacy-Aware Federated Learning Frameworks for Energy Systems within Smart Grids
abstract: The global transition towards Smart Grids (SGs) has brought about significant advancements in energy management and efficiency. To sustain these advancements, robust data-driven models trained on large-scale energy datasets are essential. However, the bidirectional flow of data and increasing connectivity within SG infrastructures have introduced cybersecurity and privacy vulnerabilities, raising concerns about the protection of sensitive consumer and operational information as well as regulatory compliance. Federated Learning (FL), a decentralized machine learning paradigm, has emerged as a promising solution to these challenges, enabling models to be trained at the edge while ensuring the accuracy of a global model. Although numerous studies have explored the application of FL in the Internet of Things (IoT), this paper presents a survey of most recent and impactful literature on the application of FL algorithms within the SG domain. Our analysis integrates findings from key studies, categorizing the primary applications of FL to address common challenges such as communication overhead and statistical heterogeneity arising from non-independently and identically distributed (non-IID) data. We also explore promising avenues for future research in FL and anomaly detection. Furthermore, we examine various FL architectures, threat models, privacy-preserving mechanisms, and the gaps in existing datasets and protocols.

title: Adoption of Smart Energy Management Applications for Smart Grids: Roles of Trust, Data Transparency, and Perceived Usefulness
abstract: Smart energy management applications have become a significant user facing service component of smart grid services, though they are yet to be adopted across users and platforms. The paper examines the motivators of Adoption Intention on smart energy management applications with the concentration on five main user perceptions pertaining to value, credibility, and service experience. The survey data were obtained from 103 participants who had previously used energy management and electricity service application. The study applies linear regression to estimate the effects of System Trust, Data Transparency, Usefulness, Security and Privacy, and Ease of Use on Adoption Intention. The results indicate that Usefulness is the strongest positive predictor of adoption intention, while System Trust and Data Transparency also have significant positive effects. Security and Privacy is positive and non-significant and Ease of Use has a marginal positive effect. The results imply that the perceived practical value and trust in the general service system are the main determinants of adoption in the context of supported by the practice of transparent data. The implications are related to the utilities and service providers interested in enhancing the uptake of the users through better value focused feature design, trust establishment, and more explicit communication of data.

title: What Data Do You Really Need? Feature-Level Privacy Analysis for Household Energy Forecasting
abstract: Accurate household energy forecasting benefits from granular smart meter data, yet the EU General Data Protection Regulation demands data minimization. Existing privacypreserving approaches (differential privacy, federated learning) protect data after collection. We ask a complementary question: which feature categories can be removed entirely before collection? We propose a feature-level privacy analysis that organizes forecasting inputs into four privacy levels, from highly invasive appliance-level activity traces to publicly available metadata. Through evaluation across three household energy datasets (Canada, France, United Kingdom), representing basic metering, circuit-level monitoring, and fully instrumented smart homes, we quantify the forecasting cost of progressively removing private data. Our results show that per-appliance traces and activity labels are removable at near-zero accuracy cost (0-3%), while energy-derived features frequently categorized as “behavioral” carry 17-19 percentage points of predictive value and leak consumption patterns equivalent to raw energy data. A standard hourly smart meter with building metadata provides near-optimal forecasting. Sub-metering hardware is not justified by accuracy gains. At the strictest privacy level, only datasets with building metadata (occupancy, house size) outperform a persistence baseline. Under the recommended collection policy, new household predictions stabilize within 6 hours of meter deployment. All findings replicate under Ridge regression, confirming model independence. These results provide empirical guidance for GDPR-compliant data minimization in smart meter infrastructure.

title: Opportunities, Characteristics and Challenges of Smart Grids
abstract: Future electricity should be flexible, accessible, reliable and economically viable for them to achieve the smart grid initiative which include the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) through increased penetration of Renewable Energy Sources (RES) such as solar, wind and other micro-sources. The grid is undergoing significant changes because of increasing demand of electricity, growing political pressure and public awareness on the need to reduce carbon emission and integrate large scale renewable power by blending information and communication technologies with power system operation which led to the microgrid concept which has evolved into smart grid technologies. Smart grids constitute an evolution of traditional grids by integrating digital communication, automation, and data analytics in the conventional grids. The smart grids offer improved efficiency and more efficient renewable integration enhanced by the two-way communication and self-healing ability. However, they face significant technical, non-technical and economic hurdles like high cots, cybersecurity risks, interoperability, privacy and confidentiality issues. Smart grids are networks employing digital communications, automated controls, and advanced sensors for optimal power generation, distribution, and use by offering efficiency, sustainability, and reliability. The conventional power grids are experiencing significant expansion which calls for reliability and efficiency in operation and maintenance to guarantee efficient and sustainable power generation, delivery and end use capable of supporting a diverse, heterogeneous operating measures and devices like smart appliances, smart meters, and renewable plug-in vehicles, energy resources generation systems supported by the grid. The growing electricity demand, expansion of the grid and high number of generating plants and customers have continuously increased the complexity and challenges of the electricity grid in delivering quality and reliable electricity to end users. These challenges require greater system reliability, improved efficiency, more security, cleaner environment and higher system sustainability can be realized by using smarter electricity grids. The smart grid is a rapidly growing concept in the electricity industry that has potential to transform the use of variable renewables variable loads and improve energy efficiency in grid power systems. The smart grid technologies have demonstrated potential to revolutionize the electricity grid by means of two-way communications to improve power system reliability, economy, efficiency, and sustainability in power generation, transmission, and distribution. The objective of this paper is to present a technical overview of smart grid first by discussing its features and capabilities followed by a discussion of the challenges, communication features, policies and regulation, and recommendations for sustainable implementation.

title: FedShield-DERMS: Federated Intrusion Detection for Smart Grids
abstract: The rapid shift to utilizing distributed energy resources (DER) in Distributed Energy Resource Management Systems (DERMS) has been accompanied by a number of cybersecurity challenges for modern smart grids. These challenges include injection of false data and denial of service attacks, as well as a number of other, more subtle, reconnaissance-based attacks. Most of the existing research in the area of intrusion detection has relied either on the collection of data at a centralized location or extensive privacy assumptions, while much of the data is composed of independent, identically distributed data. These assumptions and methodologies do not capture the interest of the highly heterogeneous smart grids. This paper reviews federated learning-based intrusion detection published between 2022 and 2026, and analyzes the proliferation of non-robust, inefficient, and adversarial frameworks with no knowledge of the DERMS communication protocols. With the goal of minimizing these gaps, we present FedShield-DERMS. FedShield-DERMS is a federated intrusion detection system composed of a lightweight, hybrid CNN-LSTM local model framework, a trust-weighted secure aggregation approach, and differential-privacy noise tailored to cover the DERMS. A controlled evaluation framework for the federated intrusion detection system is proposed to assess detection, and intrusion metrics, including communication overhead, in comparison to centralized and conventional federated approaches.

venue: 2026 3rd International Conference on Connected Innovation and Technology (ICCITX)
title: Federated Learning Attacks in Smart Grid Energy Forecasting: Threat Model, Comparative Analysis, and Impact Mapping
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted in Smart Grids to support privacy-preserving analytics across multiple stakeholders, notably for short-horizon energy forecasting such as load, PV generation, and net-load prediction. However, FL introduces a distinct attack surface through the exchange of model updates, and adversarial manipulations can propagate into operational decision errors. This paper studies the impact of major FL threat families in the specific context of Smart Grid forecasting, with an emphasis on how Smart Grid constraints (heterogeneity, non-IID data, drift, and time-critical operation) shape attack feasibility, stealth, and consequences. We first define a unified and realistic threat model for forecasting deployments. We then provide a contextualized taxonomy covering data poisoning, model poisoning, backdoor, and inference attacks, and propose a compact qualitative comparison along availability/resilience, integrity, confidentiality/privacy, and detectability. Building on this analysis, we establish an impact mapping that links machine learning (ML) failure modes (degradation, bias, trigger-conditioned errors, or leakage) to operational risks in forecasting-driven grid functions. Finally, we outline a lightweight reference framework to guide future experimental evaluations and the design of protection mechanisms for Smart Grid forecasting.

title: Cyberattack Detection in Smart Grids: A Survey of Machine Learning Approaches and Challenges
abstract: Smart Grids utilize bidirectional energy and data flows enabled by Information and Communications Technology (ICT) to create significant vulnerabilities to cyberattacks that affect grid reliability, economic performance, and public safety. Machine Learning approaches have shown potential to support intrusion detection systems; however, prior studies lack systematic comparisons across attack vectors and analyses of the deployment trade-offs associated with smart grid cybersecurity methods. By comparing various architectures across attack types, results indicate that model selection should be topology-aware. For example, Graph Neural Networks showed superior performance in detecting false data injection attacks by encoding the physical structure of the power grid, while Transformer-based models excelled in detecting electricity theft attacks by capturing long-range temporal dependencies in historical electricity consumption data. Additionally, privacy-preserving federated learning demonstrated reasonable accuracy for binary classification problems, but it has limited capability for multi-class classification, and adversarial robustness remains severely underexplored, with fewer than 7% of reviewed works testing for evasion attacks. Dataset concentration represents a major obstacle to generalizing results: nearly all false data injection literature uses IEEE synthetic systems, while theft detection relies on a single benchmark. The findings provide practitioners with evidence-based guidance for selecting architectures and researchers with a roadmap that addresses robustness, explainability, and real-world validation.

venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET)
title: Review of Privacy and Security Mechanisms in Smart Cities: From Data Protection to Threat Prevention
abstract: Privacy and cybersecurity systems in smart cities are critically reviewed and assessed in the present paper by synthesizing 21 peer-reviewed publications, published between 2018 and 2024, but the works on the topic published prior to 2018 are also acknowledged to provide background information. The paper not only classifies these mechanisms, but further compares them against the frameworks of privacy protection, scalability, governance and resilience, a separation between the technical and legal approaches. The systematic literature review was conducted based on the five-phase protocol presented by Kitchenham with the assistance of a PRISMAlike quality assessment of the studies included. These mechanisms were categorized into five themes that comprise blockchain-based architectures, intrusion detection and machine learning models, privacy-preserving learning systems, legal and governance frameworks and hybrid trust-based architectures. An evaluation lens Technology, Governance, and Resilience (TGR) triad was used to make comparative synthesis and prioritize both performance and limitation and applicability at the city level. As determined in the review, blockchain-enabled schemes dominate in the recent researches and offer immutability, auditability, but have a limitation of latency, interoperability and high power-consumption. Methods of machine learning are more accurate in detection, yet can not be interpreted or adversarial resistant. These regulations such as GDPR are enforced but not dynamic and thus, they lag behind the evolving technologies. Hybrid trust based models are promising to be integrated yet they are computationally expensive. The review has identified ten gaps, which include dynamic consent, adversarial robustness, explainable AI and cross-jurisdictional interoperability. The results indicate that scalable, modular, and legally entrenched structures are immediately required in order to balance privacy, cost, and social trust of urban infrastructures. Practice implications may be reduced costs of cybersecurity breaches, enhanced citizen trust in smart services, and advice to policymakers on how compliance may be incorporated into technical design instead of ex-post regulation. The current research is the only one that combines technological, governance and economical views into a comparative framework. It provides a resilient, privacy-conscious and economically viable roadmap towards co-designing smart city systems by placing post-2018 mechanisms in a broader historical context to guide researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to implement a coherent approach to smarter cities

The paper discusses the layered IoT architecture for smart grids, explores various wireless communications solutions including ZigBee, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT and 5G. The article also examines enabling IoT technologies including big data analysis, blockchain-based secure transactions for energy trading and federated learning for privacy preservation. Emerging IoT paradigms like blockchain-enabled DL networks, lattice-based cryptography schemes for IoT devices and software-defined vehicular edge computing solutions are analyzed as critical components of next generation secure smart grid infrastructures. Application of IoT in demand response, fault detection, renewable sources integration, and distributed energy resource management is explored systematically. Issues associated with interoperability, scalability, cyberattacks, and real-time latency are also addressed with proposed mitigation approaches. abstract: Non-Technical Losses (NTLs) from theft, metering errors, and billing irregularities continue to affect distribution utilities by reducing revenue, distorting load measurements, and complicating regulatory compliance. The deployment of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) and improved data acquisition systems has expanded the analytical options for electricity theft detection (ETD), leading to techniques ranging from statistical screening and machine learning to deep representation learning, state-estimation-based inference, and privacy-preserving computation. venue: 2026 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC)
title: Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Neural Architecture Search in Federated EVCS Security
abstract: Rapid adoption of Electric Vehicle Charging Stations (EVCS) has generated cybersecurity vulnerabilities in smart grid infrastructure, necessitating new anomaly detection systems that can react to emerging threats and protect data privacy. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data decentralized to protect privacy; however, FedAvg and FedProx use static, homogenous neural architectures that cannot adjust to client heterogeneity or changing attack patterns. Even FL Neural Architecture Search (NAS) approaches generate fixed designs per client without dynamic modification. This study proposes FedRNAS, a new framework that combines reinforcement learning (RL) with neural architecture search to enable dynamic model customization in federated environments. Our approach uses a Q-learning agent to continually update neural architectures for each client based on real-time performance feedback and changing threat scenarios. FedRNAS achieves 96.75% detection accuracy, a notable $+1.31 {\%}$ improvement over standard FedNAS, according to extensive tests conducted on four EVCS datasets from the IEEE-123 bus system. Our work is the first to demonstrate RL-driven dynamic NAS in federated learning, allowing for autonomous adaptation to emerging cybersecurity threats in critical infrastructure while keeping the privacy benefits of federated methods.

title: Cyber Security in Wireless Charging Systems for Electric Vehicles
abstract: Wireless charging technology for electric vehicles (EVs) has attracted rather significant interest because it removes the use of physical connectors, additionally promoting apparent user convenience, efficiency, and user automation within the broader transportation infrastructure system. However, wireless power transfer combined with advances in smart technologies and communication networks presents new challenges in cyber security. With electric vehicle charging systems being connected to the smart grid, integrating with the Internet of Things (IoT), and using cloud-based data storage and management, they become vulnerable to hacker attack vectors, such as eavesdropping, data manipulation, denial-of-service, and energy theft. Cyberattacks on wireless charging could result in more than just disruptions to user charging, having serious implications for user privacy, impacts on grid security and stability, and safety in the transportation system at large. This paper aims to expose the key cyber security concerns wireless charging systems face for EVs, threats and risks, and mitigation. Through a comprehensive literature review, we consider existing research, as well as identify gaps. The proposed methodology considers existing cryptographic protocols, utilize intrusion detection systems frameworks, and suggest blockchain security to promote resilience. Validation through simulation shows these techniques have efficient attack mitigation and secure energy transfer capabilities. The article concludes with recommendations for future research, urging the development of robust, scalable, and adaptive cyber security framework with respect to wireless EV charging frameworks in smart transportation ecosystems.

venue: 2026 International Conference on Electric Power and Renewable Energy (EPREC)
title: Cyber–Physical Power Systems: Attacks, Detection, and Cross-Domain Mitigation
abstract: The electrical grid’s evolution into an interconnected cyber–physical system has markedly increased its operational capabilities — and its exposure to malicious actors. This paper surveys major cyber threats across generation, transmission, distribution and device layers, then synthesizes a compact taxonomy of detection approaches ranging from physics-aware estimators to statistical and machine-learning detectors and timing-based monitors. Building on domain-specific examples (e.g., PMU manipulations, false data injection, firmware tampering and denial-of-service), we propose a layered detection architecture that integrates lightweight edge checks, local physics-consistency tests, central machine-learning ensembles, and timing integrity monitors. The proposed stack maps naturally onto the NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), providing a practical prioritization path for utilities. Finally, we identify open problems — adversarial robustness for ML detectors, low-latency authenticated protection messaging in IEC 61850 Type-1 services, and supply-chain provenance — and propose concrete near-term measures such as time-source redundancy, firmware signing, and PMU placement audits. The goal is a compact, implementable roadmap that balances rapid detection, operational latency constraints, and long-term resilience investments.

title: A Secure IoT and Machine Learning Framework using Variational Autoencoders for Intelligent Cyberattack Detection
abstract: The growing number of Internet of Things (IoT) smart ecosystems in the fields of smart healthcare, industrial automation, smart grids, and low-altitude UAV infrastructures has led to a greater exposure to attacks such as distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, port scanning, replay attacks, and zero-day intrusions. Current intrusion detection systems (IDS) for IoT networks tend to be supervised learning systems with poor generalization capabilities, and they also may demand a centralized aggregation of data that is difficult to operate in privacy-sensitive and resource-constrained settings in the edge. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces VAE-IoT CyberShield, an endowment of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and federated differential privacy, as well as edge-optimized inference for real-time IoT security analytics, to provide a lightweight and secure framework for detecting cyberattacks. The proposed framework first learns probabilistic latent representations of the normal network traffic, and then determines the anomalous behavior based on a threshold of the reconstruction error calculated using the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) method. The federated training protocol with differential privacy keeps the sensitive traffic information safe when collaborating on model optimization. Experimental results on NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, CIC-IoT2023 and Smart-Grid Telemetry datasets show that the proposed method achieves a mean detection accuracy of 97.4%, an F1-score of 0.971 and a false positive rate of 0.9%, which is superior to the state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised baselines. In addition, the compressed edge model has an inference latency of 2.1ms when running on ARM Cortex-M4 hardware, demonstrating its real-time capabilities for use in resource-constrained IoT applications.

title: Design and Implementation of Energy Consumption Forecasting using Deep Neural Networks
abstract: An accurate forecasting of energy consumption is a core need of effective energy planning, smart grid operation, and sustainable energy management. The growing supply of high-resolution data of smart meters, Internet of Things equipment, and smart energy infrastructure has speeded up the process of adopting data-driven forecasting methods. Deep neural networks are among them and have become a powerful tool as they can model such complex nonlinear association and capture long-term temporal dependence in energy consumption data. This survey is a detailed overview of energy consumption forecasting methods design and implementation using deep learning. It logically analyzes the nature of the energy consumption data, forecasting horizons and constraints of the conventional statistical methods. The paper evaluates the most popular deep neural network architectures, such as feedforward, recurrent, convolutional, hybrid and attention-based models, their strengths and usage cases. Besides, the survey talks about the practical design and implementation issues including the method of data acquisition, preprocessing, feature engineering, training plans, and consideration of deployment. The performance evaluation measures, benchmarking and comparison analysis are also evaluated. Lastly, the paper determines essential challenges, unresolved problems and research perspectives about robustness, interpretability, scalability and privacy. This survey is expected to become a useful source of information to the researchers and practitioners engaged in the work on the intelligent and sustainable energy forecasting systems.

abstract: This paper investigates the effectiveness of Deep Neural Network architectures for short-term residential energy load forecasting and compares them with conventional machine learning models. title: Explainable AI for Electric Vehicle Charging Optimization: Challenges, Opportunities, and Future Directions: A Review
abstract: The surge of electric vehicles (EVs) has heighted the demand for intelligent and efficient charging management systems that can manage energy demand, grid stability and user convenience. AI-powered charging optimization methods, such as machine learning and deep learning models, have proven to be powerful tools in predicting charging behavior, optimizing energy distribution, and integrating renewable energy sources. But the majority of AI systems are black boxes with a lack of transparency, interpretability, and trust, especially for vital energy use cases. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) tackles these challenges by offering transparent explanations to AI-driven decision-making, which enhances the reliability, accountability, and trust in EV charging systems. This review summarizes all the recent developments in EV charging optimization using XAI, including algorithms, architectures, applications, evaluation metrics, and implementation strategies. The paper also explores some of the challenges including computational complexity, scalability, privacy concerns, real-time adaptability, and standardization issues. Finally, existing research gaps are identified, future opportunities for human-centric and transparent charging systems are outlined and the real-world implications of implementing XAI-based solutions in next generation smart grids and sustainable transportation systems are stated.

abstract: The high rate of distributed intelligent system evolution has prompted the need to develop scalable, dynamic, and collaborative learning paradigms that can work in heterogeneous and decentralized environments. In this paper, I would like to introduce a new framework of multi-agent learning systems that will facilitate efficient distributed intelligence in large-scale applications. The solution proposed combines both cooperative and competitive learning schemes, reinforcement learning schemes, and decentralized optimization schemes to support autonomous decision-making between multiple interacting agents. All agents work with incomplete observability and collaboratively towards one common global goal via dynamic information exchange and coordination mechanisms. The framework uses sophisticated systems, including federated learning, graph-based communication models, and trust-aware consensus mechanisms that make it robust, preserves privacy and is scalable in distributed environments. Moreover, the system is augmented with adaptive learning of the policies and real-time feedback loops to allow continuous improvement of the system in the changing environment. The experimental analysis shows that convergence speed, system throughput, resource usage, and fault tolerance are significantly better than in conventional models of centralized and single-agent models. The suggested multi-agent learning paradigm can be used in a broad variety of fields, such as smart grids, autonomous transportation systems, distributed healthcare analytics, and intelligent supply chain management. The work would help in developing the state-of-the-art in distributed artificial intelligence by offering a complete and practical solution to the next generation intelligent system.

title: Pathways to Energy Sector Modernization: A Transition Toward Digital Public Infrastructure
abstract: The global energy sector is undergoing a profound transformation driven by the increasing integration of renewable energy sources and growing demand resulting from rapid electrification and economic expansion. Global rooftop solar capacity is expected to exceed 3,600 GW by 2035, and electricity demand is projected to nearly double by 2050. These trends highlight the structural limitations of traditional, centralized energy systems, which face increasing difficulty in managing distributed energy resources, intermittent generation, and growing demand variability. Existing infrastructures are fragmented, limited in digital capabilities, and non-interoperable, leading to inefficiencies and poor coordination across energy, information, and transaction flows. Transitioning towards a Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) is, therefore, a crucial step in the energy sector modernization. This paper examines this transition by articulating a multi-layered DPI framework and analyzing its relevance to the energy ecosystem. It examines how DPI can overcome existing structural limitations by enabling seamless integration among diverse stakeholders, technologies, and services. Furthermore, the paper explores the global perspective by reviewing major international DPI initiatives in the energy sector. The implementation of the proposed DPI framework results in improved asset visibility, reduces systemic fragmentation, and enables interoperability, allowing seamless integration and coordination across the modern energy ecosystem.

Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT), which combines Artificial Intelligence (AI) with Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, offers promising solutions for optimizing renewable energy generation, distribution, and consumption. Empathetic responses are generated by the Dialogue Engine while Safety Core, through the fine-tuning of BERT-Sentiment and DistilRoBERTa, identifies emotional distress and triggers escalation. A speech-to-text system that identifies seven vocal expressions expands the scope of multimodal emotion detection and enhances escalation prediction. Mood trend analysis is supported by a PostgreSQL relational database (Users, Conversations, Mood Log), user sessions are protected with SHA-256 hashed credentials and subsequent linked with qualitative feedback gathered via user satisfaction surveys on core quantifiable aspects (safety, empathy tagging, escalation). The findings suggest that LLM-based multimodal systems, like Emotimate, can augment emotional support safely, with privacy, ethicality, and sustained trust from users. Incorporation of dynamic weight editing and server-side timestamp normalization usability enhancement for administrators and boosting realtime emotional analytics accuracy.

title: When Behavior Becomes the Signal: Sequence-Aware Deep Anomaly Detection for Elderly Activity Monitoring
abstract: Monitoring the daily activities of elderly people living alone is a major challenge in smart healthcare systems. Non-intrusive sensing solutions based on household energy consumption have gained increasing attention due to their low deployment cost and privacy-preserving nature. However, detecting behavioral anomalies from aggregated electricity consumption remains challenging as most anomaly detection techniques fail to capture temporal dependencies inherent to human routines. This paper provides (i) a structured review of commonly used anomaly detection models in the literature, (ii) an ADL-oriented analysis of their limitations, and (iii) an experimental validation of sequence-aware deep learning using LSTM Autoencoders on the REFIT dataset. Preliminary results demonstrate that modeling temporal regularity enables effective detection of behavioral deviations in daily energy consumption patterns.

title: A Comparative Study of Environmental Sensing for Ambient Intelligence with Distributed Sensor Networks and Mobile Robots
abstract: Ambient Intelligence (AmI) systems depend on reliable environmental sensing to support comfort, safety, and energy efficiency in indoor spaces. This paper reviews three sensing paradigms for monitoring indoor environmental conditions: distributed wireless sensor networks (WSN), mobile robots employed as sensing platforms, and hybrid architectures that integrate static and mobile sensing. Typical system architectures and operational characteristics are examined, with emphasis on the trade-offs between continuous temporal monitoring at fixed locations and adaptive spatial mapping enabled by mobility. Based on this analysis, a decision framework is introduced that defines practical selection criteria including spatial and temporal requirements, cost (CAPEX/OPEX), reliability, safety, privacy, scalability, and infrastructure constraints, and illustrates how these criteria guide the choice between WSN-based, robot-based, and hybrid solutions. Finally, directions for future research are outlined, focusing on quantitative validation and software-supported methods for automated sensing architecture selection in AmI systems.

venue: IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence
title: FedSTAFN: A Secure and Efficient Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Model for Electricity Theft Detection
abstract: Detecting electricity theft is essential for promptly identifying and preventing unauthorized use of electricity, which helps in mitigating economic losses and ensuring the secure and stable operation of power systems. However, existing centralized machine learning-based detection methods still face several challenges: 1) high communication costs due to centralized data transmission, 2) significant privacy leakage risks arising from the need to aggregate sensitive user electricity data, 3) suboptimal detection accuracy caused by insufficient utilization of spatio-temporal characteristics of electricity consumption data, and 4) limited data sharing resulting from data privacy. To simultaneously address these four challenges, this study introduces a pioneering privacy-preserving framework for distributed electricity theft detection, that enjoys two-fold ideas: 1) it develops a theft detection model leveraging a Spatio-temporal Attention Fusion Network (STAFN) to enhance detection accuracy, and 2) It designs an efficient federated learning (FL) framework for model training, which enables distributed model training without aggregating raw user electricity data, directly tackling the problem of limited data sharing while reducing data transmission volume to lower communication costs. Furthermore, the framework integrates the modular additive one-time pad (MOTP) protocol for secure model aggregation, effectively mitigating privacy leakage risks during the federated training process. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed STAFN model outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in both centralized and federated learning settings, under independent and identically distributed (IID) and non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data conditions. Meanwhile, the proposed framework achieves superior performance in terms of privacy preservation, communication efficiency, and data sharing feasibility compared to traditional centralized methods.

title: QUPID: A Partitioned Quantum Neural Network for Anomaly Detection in Smart Grid
abstract: Smart grid infrastructures have revolutionized energy distribution, but their day-to-day operations require robust anomaly detection methods to counter risks associated with cyber-physical threats and system faults potentially caused by natural disasters, equipment malfunctions, and cyber attacks. Conventional machine learning (ML) models are effective in several domains, yet they struggle to represent the complexities observed in smart grid systems. Furthermore, traditional ML models are highly susceptible to adversarial manipulations, making them increasingly unreliable for real-world deployment. Quantum ML (QML) provides a unique advantage, utilizing quantum-enhanced feature representations to model the intricacies of the high-dimensional nature of smart grid systems while demonstrating greater resilience to adversarial manipulation. In this work, we propose QUPID, a partitioned quantum neural network (PQNN) that outperforms traditional state-of-the-art ML models in anomaly detection. We extend our model to R-QUPID that even maintains its performance when including differential privacy (DP) for enhanced robustness. Moreover, our partitioning framework addresses a significant scalability problem in QML by efficiently distributing computational workloads, making quantum-enhanced anomaly detection practical in large-scale smart grid environments. Our experimental results in various scenarios exemplify the efficacy of QUPID and R-QUPID to significantly improve anomaly detection capabilities and robustness compared to traditional ML approaches.

title: Pricing Appliance Usage Privacy for Enhancing Usability of Smart Meter Data
abstract: Consumers’ privacy concerns often limit the usage of their smart meter data in several data-driven applications. While privacy-preserving algorithms can address the privacy concerns of consumers, these algorithms erase useful information; thus reducing the data usability. Data usability can be enhanced if the utility can directly utilize the smart meter data of consumers without transforming the same using privacy-preserving algorithms. However, this is not possible unless consumers give up their privacy rights over their smart meter data. Offering monetary compensations to consumers can be a possible approach to encourage them to give up the privacy rights over their smart meter data. Hence, this paper proposes a novel privacy pricing method that monetarily compensates the loss of appliance usage privacy incurred by the consumers who agreed to give up the privacy rights over their smart meter data. At first, a consumer’s appliance usage privacy is modeled based on how the consumer’s consumptions fluctuate over a given time period. Then, a nonlinear convex optimization problem is proposed using the privacy model to determine the privacy prices of a set of consumers under a given budget of the utility. The properties of the optimal solution are demonstrated mathematically. It is shown that the practical implementation of the proposed pricing method is unlikely to impact the consumption patterns of consumers. The impacts of the utility’s budget and the number of participating consumers on the privacy prices are illustrated using practical smart meter data while considering heterogeneity in the privacy concerns of consumers. Further, a novel metric is proposed which shows that, unlike the existing pricing methods, the privacy prices generated by the proposed method are sufficient to address the privacy concerns of most of the participating consumers.

title: Leveraging Solar Panels for Robust Cost-Friendly Privacy Preservation of Smart Meters
abstract: Analyzing high-resolution data from smart meters (SMs) enables the identification of internal household activities and even personal user information, posing a significant privacy threat to energy consumers. Thus, preserving SM’s privacy is paramount. While data tampering methods offer a solution, they often lead to issues such as inaccurate state estimation and complex billing. To address this, we propose demand-side energy management leveraging rechargeable batteries (RBs) and solar panels. This is because larger RBs are costly and environmentally unfriendly. Thus, we prioritize the use of green energy sources, such as solar panels, minimizing RB’s reliance on enhanced consumer privacy. Strategically managing loads with solar panels and grid energy sales achieves cost-effective privacy. Considering realistic off-peak and peak energy consumption periods renders our approach practical. Theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Privacy-Preserving Multi-Agent Deep Evolutionary Learning for Decentralized Emergency Control
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising methodological framework for power grid emergency control tasks in the past few years, for its advantages in real-time response capability and complex relationship mapping. However, its application to the decentralized emergency control problem is still challenging, due to the computational complexity, scalability, and privacy limitations of state-of-the-art multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) approaches. To fill these gaps, this paper proposes a novel multi-agent deep evolutionary learning method (MADEL) for decentralized emergency control. Unlike conventional MADRL methods, the proposed MADEL method trains the agents by performing population-based parameter space exploration and eliminates the guidance of centralized Critic networks, which not only avoids the credit assignment issue, but also contributes to lower computational complexity and better scalability. Furthermore, when confronted with multi-area power systems, a novel cloud-edge collaborative distributed training paradigm is tailored for MADEL to achieve data privacy protection during offline training. Numerical simulations on the IEEE 39-bus system and a 3-area 117-bus system confirm the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

title: From Measurement to Monitoring: Evaluating Privacy Risks in Carbon Footprint Tools
abstract: The increasing urgency of climate change mitigation has accelerated the adoption of tools to measure and monitor greenhouse gas emissions at individual, organizational, and infrastructural levels. While these tools enhance the accuracy and accountability of emissions measurement, they also raise privacy concerns due to the sensitive data they collect, the granularity of monitoring, and the potential for secondary use. Despite their growing adoption, no prior study has systematically evaluated the privacy implications of carbon footprint tools across categories or examined how data practices differ between consumer calculators, enterprise systems, and emerging Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and blockchain solutions. This study addresses this gap by conducting a structured, cross-category privacy evaluation of carbon footprint tools, reviewing 46 tools from academic and industry sources. A novel five-dimensional privacy risk framework, encompassing data type, granularity, storage, processing, secondary use, and user agency, is developed and applied across five tool categories: individual calculators, corporate platforms, infrastructure tools, IoT/AI/blockchain systems, and research tools. The findings reveal pronounced privacy-accuracy trade-offs: tools offering higher measurement precision often require more intrusive data collection. The study also identifies category-specific least- and highest-risk tools, showing that simple household calculators present low risk. In contrast, enterprise platforms and IoT/blockchain systems exhibit the highest exposure due to sensitive operational, financial, and real-time data flows. The study is limited by its reliance on literature and public documentation, suggesting the need for empirical field studies and technical audits. Future research should expand on these findings by investigating user perceptions, legal frameworks, and privacy-preserving design strategies for sustainable digital tools.

title: Collusion-Resistant Privacy-Preserving Multidimensional Data Aggregation Scheme With Dynamic Membership for the Industrial Internet of Things
abstract: As industrial devices in the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) generate increasing amounts of sensing data, privacy-preserving aggregation has become essential for efficient data collection and analysis in practical industrial environments. However, most existing privacy-preserving data aggregation schemes assume static device participation, lack resistance to collusion attacks between aggregators and data centers (DCs), and incur high computational overhead due to the use of bilinear pairing operations. To overcome these limitations, this article introduces a privacy-preserving multidimensional data aggregation (PPMDA) scheme with dynamic device participation support. In each data encryption process, each sensor node (SN) uses its private key, the public keys of the adjacent SNs, and a time parameter to generate a blinding factor to hide its data, eliminating the need for a trusted third party to preset the blinding factor. Importantly, the scheme supports dynamic device participation, enabling devices to join or leave the system without requiring system reinitialization or disrupting ongoing data aggregation. Security analysis confirms that PPMDA ensures data privacy and authentication while defending against collusive attacks on edge servers (ESs) and DCs. By avoiding pairing operations, PPMDA significantly reduces computational overhead compared to five existing schemes, making it a practical and efficient solution for large-scale and dynamically evolving IIoT environments.

venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
title: On the Attribute Hiding Security of Privacy Preserving Secret-Sharing-Based Outsourced Decision Tree Classification
abstract: Decision tree classification serves as a fundamental component in many machine learning applications. As inference services are increasingly outsourced to cloud platforms, designing privacy-preserving mechanisms has become important. To secure outsourced decision tree inference, Chen et al. proposed SecDT, an efficient secret-sharing-based framework. While SecDT offers notable efficiency and preliminary security guarantees, we identify a critical vulnerability: attribute leakage. Specifically, the attributes associated with decision tree nodes are exposed to non-owner parties, which risks revealing sensitive model information. In this paper, we first present two secure enhancements, SecDT+v1 and SecDT+v2. These variants use the transformation matrix technique to obfuscate node attributes within the secret-shared domain. To prevent more advanced leakage through attribute access patterns, we design two advanced variants, SecDT+vH and SecDT+vDP, which incorporate dot-product operations to achieve the attribute-hiding property. Extensive evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed schemes provide robust security guarantees while outperforming state-of-the-art solutions in both classification latency and bandwidth efficiency.

venue: IEEE Transactions on Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems
title: Confidence-Aware Federated Learning for Smart Load Characterization in Cyber-Physical DER Systems
abstract: The integration of smart meters into residential environments has allowed smooth collection of electricity consumption data, which is critical for demand response and coordinated operation in cyber-physical distributed energy resource systems. However, existing centralized methods of consumer characteristic identification pose significant risks to data privacy and confidentiality. Furthermore, the inherent limitations imposed due to noisy data cause a steep degradation in the accuracy and system-level decision-making. Addressing the issues of accuracy and data confidentiality, this paper proposes a confidence-aware federated learning framework for privacy-preserving inference of electricity consumer characteristics from raw smart meter data. The proposed method employs decentralized retention of smart meter data, using federated learning to refine network performance while ensuring that raw data remain localized at the client level. By evaluating a combined distribution of noisy and clean labels, erroneous data points are identified and excluded, thereby enhancing the model's efficacy and robustness. The effectiveness of the approach is validated using the Irish Commission for Energy Regulation dataset. The proposed framework demonstrates notable improvements, achieving an average gain of 3.97% in accuracy and 3.68% in MCC score compared to state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining strong data privacy guarantees.

venue: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
title: Time Period Selected Aggregation for Providing Hierarchical and Differentiated Services in Mobile Sensing
abstract: With the advancement of smart terminals and wireless networking technologies, mobile sensing has gained increasing popularity. A myriad of applications have emerged based on mobile sensing, with particular attention being drawn to data aggregation applications. Over the years, numerous studies have been conducted, ranging from initial approaches that did not address the issue of untrusted aggregators to more recent solutions capable of handling such challenges. In this paper, we introduce two novel types of data aggregation applications designed to offer hierarchical and differentiated services, alongside proposing two corresponding protocols equipped with privacy-preserving capabilities. These protocols ensure the protection of mobile users’ privacy concerning their sensed data in the presence of an untrusted aggregator, and are resilient against collusion attacks. Our protocols achieve constant key storage overhead (only 1 key per user), in stark contrast to other state-of-the-art schemes where the overhead grows linearly with the number of service levels. We perform a performance analysis of the proposed protocols using the building block protocol as a benchmark, which demonstrates their efficiency: each mobile user incurs a total energy cost of approximately 62.0 mJ per reporting round, with an average end-to-end aggregation latency of less than 10 milliseconds, demonstrating that the proposed protocols can be used in practical settings. While the proposed protocols rely on a trusted authority, a common assumption in existing privacy-preserving aggregation schemes, future work will explore decentralized key management to support fully trustless environments.

venue: Journal of Modern Power Systems and Clean Energy
title: Cybersecurity in Virtual Power Plants: A Review of Theoretical Framework, Risk Analysis, and Defense Technologies
abstract: Virtual power plants (VPPs) can participate in electricity market trading by aggregating distributed energy resources, thereby providing flexible regulation services to the power system. However, the interaction between VPPs and the power system involves high-frequency and multi-party data exchange, posing significant cybersecurity risks. To ensure the cybersecurity of VPPs throughout the entire interaction process, this paper first analyzes the intrinsic attributes of VPPs, identifying three key characteristics: aggregation, interaction, and regulation. Based on this, it integrates these attributes with confidentiality, integrity, and availability triad to construct a cyber-security theoretical framework for VPPs. Second, this paper outlines the business processes, data interactions, and communication architecture of VPPs. Then, a risk analysis of potential cyberattacks is performed, detailing their injection points, propagation paths, and potential impacts of typical cyberattacks. Third, the core application mechanisms and use cases of key cybersecurity defense technologies are summarized. These technologies are applicable to interactions between VPP and power systems across different stages, including data anonymization, encryption, privacy-preserving computation, access control, and blockchain. Finally, an analysis of the current status, challenges, and prospects of artificial intelligence (AI)-based cybersecurity technologies is presented, which provides support for constructing a secure and reliable cybersecurity defense system for VPPs.

title: Evaluating the Timeliness of Cryptography for Securing ICS Protocols in Smart Grid
abstract: For a safe and reliable power system, secure communication is crucial. Industrial control system (ICS) protocols, which play an important role in power grid communication, were designed decades ago without any built-in security techniques. Exploiting vulnerabilities in such protocols could result in unauthorized access, data manipulation and even lead to severe consequences such as complete blackouts of the power grid. Thus, the legacy ICS protocols utilized in smart grid communications should be transformed into secure protocols to mitigate cyberattacks. The fundamental building blocks to achieve security in the ICS protocols, covering confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation lie in cryptography. This paper explores where the major cryptographic algorithms, such as stream ciphers, block ciphers, elliptic-curve cryptography schemes, hash functions and authenticated encryption stand when they are used to secure the ICS protocols, in terms of performance and cost, while balancing the inherent characteristics of the smart grid environments such as strict time and resource constraints. We extensively evaluate a range of contemporary cryptographic schemes and analyze their effectiveness in smart grid communication. We analyze the performance of these cryptographic primitives on both hardware (FPGA-based) and software (microcontroller-based) platforms, assessing their impact on system efficiency and security. This study will be invaluable for researchers in the smart grid domain in selecting cipher suites according to the development platform (hardware or software) to ensure the optimal balance between performance and security.

venue: IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement
title: Bridging Distributional Gaps in High-Resolution Load Profile Records via Latent-Perturbation Generative Framework
abstract: The high-resolution load profiles acquired by the advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) are essential for the precise monitoring, modeling, and operational decision-making of modern power systems. However, comprehensive acquisition of these records is often limited by sensing costs, limited communication bandwidth, and strict privacy regulations, leading to datasets that may not fully represent the underlying physical phenomenon. While generative models offer a potential solution for data augmentation, existing methods predominantly focus on replicating observed distributions, thereby neglecting critical distributional gaps containing valid but underrepresented load patterns. To address these challenges, this article proposes a novel load profile synthesis framework termed latent-perturbation maximum mean discrepancy variational autoencoder (LP-MVAE). The framework is specifically designed to bridge distributional gaps by balancing signal fidelity with exploratory diversity. By synergizing an enhanced maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) annealing strategy with an  $\varepsilon $ -ball constrained perturbation mechanism, the model shapes a continuous latent manifold while enabling controlled local exploration of unobserved or underrepresented profiles. Experimental validation on two real-world datasets demonstrates that LP-MVAE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving sample diversity by up to 10.98 % and the valid distributional coverage (VDC) composite score by up to 35.07 % over the strongest baseline. Qualitative assessments further confirm that the synthesized profiles effectively populate distributional gaps while preserving realistic temporal dynamics and physical validity.

title: Cybersecurity and data privacy in smart grids
abstract: The chapter presents the important concerns of cybersecurity and data privacy in the contemporary smart grids, which have become increasingly the foundation of the energy systems of the future. As the use of digital communication, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, renewable energy, and real-time monitoring expands, smart grids are at risk due to a broad array of threats, including the transmission of information, false data injection, denial of service, and integrity breaches. The chapter identifies five major problem areas that have developed over the recent years: strong security vs. high performance, privacy in data sharing, large-scale attacks, protection of resource-constrained edge devices, and global interoperability. It also reviews modern methods such as blockchain, zero-knowledge proofs, lightweight cryptography, federated learning, and hardware-assisted security. Although these technologies are offering partial solutions, gaps exist in the cost, scalability, and cost standardization. Much attention is also paid to policy and regulatory issues and the necessity of the global compliance framework that will coordinate privacy and security demands on an international scale. Finally, future research directions to be pursued by the chapter include post-quantum cryptography, adaptive authentication, which can be achieved through artificial intelligence (AI) and hybrid architectures that involve central and edge security strategies. The most important need of sustainable, secure smart grids is the trade-off between efficiency, privacy, and resilience.

title: Data-Driven Intelligence for Smart Grids: A State-of-the-Art Review and Future Perspectives
abstract: ABSTRACT Context Rapid breakthroughs in computing technologies and the growing availability of diverse, heterogeneous data in smart grids have driven a strong push to adopt advanced intelligence techniques. Furthermore, the increasing demand for accurate and reliable green energy forecasting has only accelerated this shift. Smart grid scenarios are no longer simple power networks; they comprise multiple distributed energy sources (DES), sensor-dependent monitoring systems, cybersecurity protocols, demand-side management (DSM) strategies, and complex communication infrastructure. Managing all these integrated components in real-time is not an easy task. Making judgments in such environments must account for a wide range of challenges, including grid stability, power quality issues, energy forecasting, anomaly detection, efficient energy management, and the rising threat of cyberattacks. Objectives In this study, we aim to explore the role of intelligent techniques in handling the emerging challenges of smart power systems regarding four major concerns, such as generation & load forecasting, energy management, fault/anomaly identification, and stability & cyber security. The primary objective of this review is to highlight and compare several existing data-driven applications, methodologies, performance evaluation metrics, limitations, and future directions, along with opportunities for reliable, scalable, and real-time smart grid primary applications. It also provides researchers with a structural understanding of the present state of the art while identifying potential prospects for subsequent advancements. Methods A systematic survey of existing research studies regarding smart grids was conducted and found that intelligent techniques consistently focus on addressing critical and complex challenges in the field. This study systematically analyzes the algorithms, model architectures, evaluation strategies, and operational challenges across the reviewed literature. The review revealed that data-based machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) models strengthen the ability of smart grids to handle large volumes of data and perform accurate real-time predictions to improve load forecasting accuracy, enable fault detection, and enhance grid stability. This work also proposes privacy-preserving, explainable solutions for smart grid challenges. Results This work provides multidimensional quick comparisons and visualization tools from generic to application-specific. It summarizes strengths, limitations, challenges, and gaps found in classic ML and complex DL models. This also provides key insights into various emerging techniques to address future challenges, focusing on scalability, interpretability, and real-time applicability. Conclusion This review offers a comparative critical analysis spanning multiple smart grid domains using various classic and explainable artificial intelligence (AI) approaches. This broader perspective helps researchers to identify the most promising solutions while also pointing to existing research gaps that can guide them to carry their future work in more targeted directions with clear objectives.

title: A Review of Cybersecurity Issues in Smart Meter-Based Energy Trading
abstract: Smart meters increasingly operate as grid-edge sensing and communication nodes, extending their role beyond conventional digital billing by generating records for local energy trading. In such settings, smart meter-derived records may support coordination, participant interaction, validation, billing, and settlement across different trading architectures. Once these records leave the metering edge, their security and privacy risks depend on how they are routed, reused, protected, and interpreted across centralized, transactive, and peer-to-peer trading workflows. In this review, we examine smart meter-based energy trading through a record-centric and framework-oriented lens. We first clarify the role of smart meters and smart meter-derived records, then compare three representative trading frameworks in terms of data-path structure, coordination pattern, trust organization, and validation or settlement positioning. Building on the comparison, we identify three lifecycle-based layers of issues: record integrity and temporal consistency, insecure transmission and interface access security, and confidentiality and privacy exposure. We also review existing mitigation mechanisms and remaining limitations for each issue layer. We conclude that future work should prioritize lifecycle-wide record governance, temporal continuity, privacy-accountability co-design, and deployable protection across hybrid trading environments.

title: Intelligent Fault Detection and Diagnostic Systems for Electric Smart Meters Using ML and AI Algorithms: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Smart meters have become the focus of electricity distribution management as the global deployment of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) has surpassed 1.7 billion installations worldwide, with projections reaching 3.4 billion units by 2033 [1]. As meter populations scale, the volume and complexity of fault detection, anomaly detection, and diagnostic classification tasks increase proportionally. Threshold-based and rule-based fault detection techniques exhibit well-documented limitations when applied to high-dimensional, non-stationary, and class-imbalanced data streams characteristic of modern AMI networks. This paper presents a systematic and comprehensive review of peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2026 on machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI)-based fault detection and diagnostic systems for electric smart meters. A structured search of IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 28 articles satisfying stringent inclusion criteria. The resulting taxonomy classifies approaches into five categories: (1) supervised learning with classical ML classifiers; (2) deep learning models including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks; (3) hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures; (4) unsupervised and semi-supervised anomaly detectors; and (5) federated and privacy-preserving learning frameworks. Systematic comparison of key performance measures—detection accuracy, F1-score, area under the ROC curve (AUC), and false-positive rate (FPR)—reveals that CNN-LSTM hybrid architectures achieve peak detection accuracies of 98.5%, while classical models such as support vector machines (SVM) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) offer consistent performance with lower computational overhead. Critical open challenges—including the absence of standardised benchmark datasets, class imbalance, adversarial robustness, edge deployment constraints, and model interpretability—are identified and discussed. Directions for future explainable, privacy-aware, and computationally efficient fault diagnostic systems are proposed.
